title: The Canadian Clearview AI Investigation as a Call for Digital Policy Literacy
thesis: Argues that digital policy literacy (DPL) is needed to critically understand privacy issues from Clearview AI, moving beyond individualist approaches to privacy.
theme_1_justification: Not addressed; no discussion of dual-use information goods or technology transfer between civilian and military domains.
theme_2_justification: Substantive engagement with epistemic authority and black-boxing via discussion of big data epistemologies, algorithmic opacity, biometric fallacy, and racial bias in facial recognition.
theme_3_justification: Not addressed; no discussion of urban modulation or programmable city.
theme_4_justification: Not addressed; no discussion of spatial destruction, home unmaking, or vertical sovereignty.
key_quotes: Rob Kitchin (2014: 2) has argued, big data thus involves new epistemologies where 'rather than testing a theory by analysing relevant data, new data analytics seek to gain insights 'born from the data.''
biometric identification technologies such as facial recognition software can enact significant harms in their inherent misidentifications
the solutions proposed to deal with these problems reflect a narrow version of digital literacy that would benefit from the expanded concerns of the DPL model
policy_relevance: Calls for stronger privacy laws, regulatory reform (Bill C-27), and a digital policy literacy framework that goes beyond individual consent to address political-economic and infrastructural dimensions of surveillance.
notes: Paper is a journal article; no truncation issues.
